item.title: Banned Pesticides: Can Anses Really Say No?
item.comments: Referred to Anses in late August 2026, the agency has two months to rule on acetamiprid and flupyradifurone, banned since 2018: can it really say no to them?
item.category: 🟢 Anses Refuses the Derogation, Citing Insufficient Guarantees","🔵 Anses Grants the Derogation, But Only for the Crops the Law Covers","🔴 The Derogation Expands Beyond What the Law Allows
item.description:
The question: Referred to Anses in late August 2026, the agency has two months to rule on acetamiprid and flupyradifurone, banned since 2018: can it really say no to them?

The facts: The emergency farming law, validated by the Constitutional Council on August 14, 2026 and enacted on August 19, allows Anses to grant a temporary derogation for acetamiprid and flupyradifurone, two pesticides banned in France since 2018, for 4 struggling farming sectors (hazelnut, apple, cherry, sugar beet).

The 3 scenarios:
🟢 Anses Refuses the Derogation, Citing Insufficient Guarantees
🔵 Anses Grants the Derogation, But Only for the Crops the Law Covers
🔴 The Derogation Expands Beyond What the Law Allows

Which one is most likely? 👉 Read the 3 numbered forecasts on the site — it's free (~5 min read).

item.source:
Can Anses really refuse to re-authorize two banned pesticides, as promised by the law that hands it this decision?
The emergency farming law, validated by the Constitutional Council on August 14, 2026 and enacted on August 19, allows Anses to grant a temporary derogation for acetamiprid and flupyradifurone, two pesticides banned in France since 2018, for 4 struggling farming sectors (hazelnut, apple, cherry, sugar beet).
The most likely scenario (45%): Anses grants the derogation exactly within the scope set by the law, for a maximum of three years, without expanding it further.
Signal to watch: Anses's decision, expected by late October 2026, two months after being referred the case by the Agriculture Minister.
Our assessment of the impact on France: fairly negative. The stable scenario (45%) and the degraded scenario (30%) both bring pesticides banned on health and environmental grounds back into French fields, at least partly — against just a 25% chance that Anses holds the line and refuses the derogation.

item.comments: Eight months from the first round, Marine Le Pen leads every poll (33-38%): can France's still-divided right and left field a candidate able to beat her in the runoff?

item.source:
Eight months from the vote, can either camp finally unite to offer a real choice against the RN, which leads the polls by a wide margin?
Between August 18 and 28, 2026, three pollsters put Marine Le Pen (or Jordan Bardella) between 33% and 38% in the first round of the 2027 presidential election, far ahead of a right and left still divided among several candidates.
The most likely scenario (50%): the current fragmentation drags on to the vote, and whoever qualifies against the RN in the runoff loses by margins close to today's polls, around 46-54%.
Signal to watch: the outcome of the left-wing primary on October 9-10 and 16-17, 2026, and any announced deal between Édouard Philippe and Bruno Retailleau on the right.
Our assessment of the impact on France: fairly negative. The stable scenario (50%) and the degraded scenario (30%) both leave France in unresolved political fragmentation, against just a 20% chance that either camp finally unites to offer a clear choice.

item.title: Iceland: After the No to the EU, Who Will Protect It?
item.comments: On August 29, 52.8% of Icelanders rejected reopening EU membership talks, while Donald Trump keeps up the pressure on neighboring Greenland. Without the EU and without an army of its own, can Iceland durably secure its position in the Arctic by relying on the United States and NATO — or will that choice isolate it further as strategic appetites for the region keep growing?

After saying no to the EU, can Iceland durably secure its place in the Arctic by relying on the United States and NATO?
On August 29, 52.8% of Icelanders rejected reopening EU membership talks, in a climate strained by Donald Trump's pressure on neighboring Greenland.
The most likely scenario (45%): Iceland stays in the same dependence on a 75-year-old American defense treaty, with no new guarantee despite growing tensions over the Arctic.
Signal to watch: the actual timeline of the NATO Helguvik base extension, planned for late 2026, and any new American announcement on Greenland in the coming months.
Our assessment of the impact on France: slightly negative. The two most likely scenarios combined (70%, stable and degraded) leave the North Atlantic in a fragile or degraded security state, only partly offset by the favorable scenario (30%), which stays a minority outcome.

item.title: Ligue 1: Can French Football Survive the Collapse of Its TV Rights?
item.comments: After the collapse of TV rights and the ongoing decline in clubs' resources, will Ligue 1 find a stable economic model, muddle through at this reduced level, or see several clubs sink into financial trouble?
item.category: 🟢 The league's own channel beats its targets","🔵 Clubs get by, but with no more money","🔴 Several clubs are relegated over unpaid bills
item.description:
The question: After the collapse of TV rights and the ongoing decline in clubs' resources, will Ligue 1 find a stable economic model, muddle through at this reduced level, or see several clubs sink into financial trouble?

The facts: Since Mediapro's collapse in 2020 and DAZN's departure in 2025, Ligue 1's domestic TV rights have been cut by more than a factor of five: clubs shared just €80.5 million net for the 2025-2026 season, against roughly €500 million a season before the crisis.

The 3 scenarios:
🟢 The league's own channel beats its targets
🔵 Clubs get by, but with no more money
🔴 Several clubs are relegated over unpaid bills

item.source:
Can French professional football find a stable economic model after the collapse of its TV rights?
Since Mediapro's collapse in 2020 and DAZN's departure in 2025, Ligue 1's domestic TV rights have been cut by more than a factor of five: clubs shared just €80.5 million net for the 2025-2026 season, against roughly €500 million a season before the crisis.
The most likely scenario (45%): Ligue 1+, the league's own channel, keeps growing slowly toward 1.2 to 1.3 million subscribers without ever reaching profitability, while clubs keep managing their books under very tight constraints, with no fresh wave of bankruptcies.
Signal to watch: Ligue 1+'s subscriber count when the international break resumes in November 2026, and the DNCG's rulings on clubs' projected accounts.
Our assessment of the impact on France: fairly negative. The two most likely scenarios combined (80%, stable and degraded) keep or worsen a league that's already well below its pre-crisis funding level — only the favorable scenario (20%) would reverse that trajectory.

item.title: Global Cinema: Can It Survive Streaming?
item.comments: Studios have set a new common rule: 45 days of theatrical exclusivity before streaming. The global box office is aiming for its best year since 2019, but major theater chains remain deep in debt, and younger audiences increasingly prefer to wait for streaming. Will this truce be enough to save theaters for good?
item.category: 🟢 The 45-day deal holds and gets longer","🔵 The 45-day deal holds, but goes no further","🔴 A studio breaks ranks, windows shrink again
item.description:
The question: Studios have set a new common rule: 45 days of theatrical exclusivity before streaming. The global box office is aiming for its best year since 2019, but major theater chains remain deep in debt, and younger audiences increasingly prefer to wait for streaming. Will this truce be enough to save theaters for good?

The facts: The global theatrical box office is targeting $34.7 billion in 2026, its best year since 2019, driven by an unprecedented agreement among studios to keep every film in exclusive theatrical release for 45 days before streaming.

The 3 scenarios:
🟢 The 45-day deal holds and gets longer
🔵 The 45-day deal holds, but goes no further
🔴 A studio breaks ranks, windows shrink again

item.source:
Can movie theaters keep holding their ground against streaming?
The global theatrical box office is targeting $34.7 billion in 2026, its best year since 2019, driven by an unprecedented agreement among studios to keep every film in exclusive theatrical release for 45 days before streaming.
The most likely scenario (45%): the 45-day deal holds exactly as is, with no further progress, and the global box office plateaus between $34 and $36 billion, without catching up to the 2019 level.
Signal to watch: Universal's announced move to seven weekends of exclusivity (about 49 days) planned for 2027, and the year-end financial results of the major theater chains (AMC, Cineworld/Regal).
Our assessment of the impact on France: fairly positive. The two most likely scenarios combined (75%, favorable and stable) extend the best year for French theaters since 2019 — only the degraded scenario (25%), which would break the window deal, would threaten that momentum.
